fullText:
Donald Trump presented Elon Musk with the top US science medal on Thursday, as the rocket tycoon fully returned to the president's orbit after an explosive bust-up.

Six US tech titans received prestigious awards from the president at a Washington peace institute that was itself recently renamed after Trump.

But all eyes were on trillionaire SpaceX and Tesla boss Musk following his acrimonious departure from Trump's cost-cutting Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) last year.

Trump called Musk a "national treasure" and said that "Elon is our modern-day Thomas Edison," referring to the American inventor of the lightbulb.

"Elon, I want to congratulate you. You're my friend, and all of that, but you are a very, very special guy," Trump added at the summit, dubbed "Science: A New Golden Age.

Along with Musk, Google co-founder Sergei Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and AMD chief Lisa Su all received the National Medal of Science from Trump during the ceremony.

Computer mogul Michael Dell and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella got the National Medal of Technology and Innovation, also the top US award in its field.

Trump and Musk gave an amiable if awkward performance on Thursday, with president patting the tycoon on the back and giving him a wooden case containing his medal. The pair largely avoided eye contact.

It was a far cry from May 2025 when Musk's brief and tempestuous time at DOGE flamed out over his opposition to the White House's "utterly insane" tax and spending bill.

Musk -- the biggest donor to Trump's 2024 presidential campaign -- had spent months working out of a small office in the White House complex as DOGE took a hatchet to the federal workforce and agencies.

He appeared at Trump's side in cabinet meetings and brought his young son X into the Oval Office alongside the president.

After they fell out, relations between the world's most powerful person and its richest person quickly turned bitter.

Trump threatened to deport the South African-born Musk, while Musk, who also owns the X social media platform, alleged links between Trump and late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

But Musk has returned to the fold in recent months, and his SpaceX rockets have continued to be a lynchpin of the US space and defense program.

He attended Trump's state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping in September and then joined talks on artificial intelligence at the White House last week.

Musk, Huang and other leaders promised at that meeting to self-regulate against possible threats from artificial intelligence.

Trump has rejected calls for government oversight, dismissing warnings that AI could wipe out humanity and insisting it is crucial for what he calls the "Golden Age" of the US economy in his second term.

Earlier Thursday, Trump said that anyone who does not use the term "super intelligence" -- the term he wants people to use instead of AI -- will be treated as "THE ENEMY."

At the medal event, Trump himself was presented with a frame containing the National Medal of Science posthumously awarded to his late uncle John Trump, a professor at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

Trump's uncle, who died in 1983, is a familiar character in Trump's speeches.

The 80-year-old president often says he inherited what he calls the "highest of IQs" from his uncle, citing "good genes."

fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The union representing thousands of flight attendants said Wednesday it has safety concerns about President Donald Trump's proposed triumphal arch that will be on final approach to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.

Association of Flight Attendants-CWA President Sara Nelson said the 250-foot (76 meter) arch compounds multiple safety concerns that she said have gone unaddressed from a deadly January 2025 crash over the Potomac River that killed 67 people. Nelson also criticized Trump's plan to turn the arch into "a top grade military complex" able to host drones and snipers while storing ammunition.

"DCA is already stretched to its limit, we do not need an obstacle taking up space in our flight path," said Nelson. "Nor should commercial aviation have to dodge military drones, missiles or snipers while attempting to take off or land at Washington National Airport. Safety first always."

Nelson's statement on behalf of the union, which represents 55,000 flight attendants across 20 airlines, joins the voices of an assemblage of veterans' groups, Congress members and others with safety concerns and complaints about the memorial's threat to historic and symbolic sightlines between different landmarks in Washington, D.C.

Though the arch has received early approval from the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts, whose members were all tapped by Trump, a group of three veterans and an architectural historian sued, saying the project needs to be approved by Congress.

Last month, the Republican president said in a social media post that he had agreed, at the "strong request" of the military, to convert the planned 250-foot-tall (76-meter) memorial arch "into a top grade Military Complex."

The Federal Aviation Administration said last month before Trump's announcement on it becoming a military complex that the arch would not pose a hazard to aircraft, but it should be "appropriately marked with a non-standard eternal flame on top of the structure and floodlight projectors pointed towards the arch to make it noticeable for pilots.

An assessment by the National Park Service said the memorial arch could disrupt the historical significance of dozens of nearby sites. The Park Service approved the project despite its assessment.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced early last month that excavation work on the site in Memorial Circle would begin within weeks. The Interior Department did not respond immediately to questions on the status of that work.

The arch is one of several projects around Washington that Trump has undertaken as he remakes the city, from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.

This story has been updated to correct the union's name. It is the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA , not Flight Attendants Association-CWA.

   Taxpayer-funded television ads glorifying Trump began airing in late September, sparking a bipartisan backlash. 
   In a post on his Truth Social site on Monday, Trump said he considered the ads to be "a positive promotion for ‌our Great U.S.
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Oct 7 (Reuters) - Democratic Party officials sued US President Donald Trump on Wednesday, seeking a court order blocking his administration from ‌using taxpayer money to pay for election-related TV ads.

The lawsuit, filed by ‌the Democratic National Committee in federal court in Washington, accused Trump of a "blatant violation of the statutory ​ban on the use of appropriations for 'publicity or propaganda purposes.'"

Taxpayer-funded television ads glorifying Trump began airing in late September, sparking a bipartisan backlash.

In a post on his Truth Social site on Monday, Trump said he considered the ads to be "a positive promotion for ‌our Great U.S.A." but that ⁠they would no longer be funded by taxpayers. The White House said this week his MAGA PAC would fund the ads.

The ⁠DNC, the main governing organization of the Democratic Party, said in its lawsuit that the ads continued to air after Trump's comments.

"With less than 30 days remaining before the midterm ​election ​and millions of public dollars apportioned to pay ​for propaganda ads still unspent, ‌the DNC has no choice but to take action in defense of free and fair elections," the lawsuit stated.

The ads ran during football games as recently as Sunday and during other programming. The New York Times reported that Trump personally directed the White House budget director to use taxpayer money for the TV spots, citing sources.

One ‌ad features Trump declaring that "America will never be ​a communist country" while a chorus repeats the ​words "love me." Another combines images of ​Mount Rushmore with footage of Trump praising a "golden age of ‌America."

Another new ad recently has featured ousted ​Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro. ​A source briefed on the matter told Reuters the government-funded ads will end this week.

The White House said Trump's political action committee will not reimburse ​taxpayers for the ads ‌that have run to date.

The ads end with a disclaimer saying they ​were paid for by the US government.

title: GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers breaks with Trump and calls to end Canada tariffs
description:
WASHINGTON — Republican U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers appears to be breaking with President Donald Trump on another key issue less than a month before Election Day.
"Drinking a Labatt and watching the Red Wings, man, it just doesn't get any more Michigan than that," Rogers said in a new ad released Oct. 7.
fullText:
WASHINGTON — Republican U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers appears to be breaking with President Donald Trump on another key issue less than a month before Election Day.

"Drinking a Labatt and watching the Red Wings, man, it just doesn't get any more Michigan than that," Rogers said in a new ad released Oct. 7. "Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now."

The statement marks the second time in recent weeks that Rogers spoke out — without criticizing Trump by name — against one of the president's unpopular initiatives. This time, Rogers is calling for an end to Trump's widespread trade war against Canada, America's second-biggest trading partner, while drinking a Canadian beer that's banned from import under the president's latest trade restrictions.

The Republican Senate nominee also split with Trump on the Iran war in late September, saying it "needs to end and end quickly."

Rogers' public shift on tariffs comes amid mounting opposition in Michigan to Trump's tariffs and GOP concerns that voters will reject their candidates up and down the ballot for failing to address cost-of-living concerns. Election Day is Nov. 3, though more than 200,000 Michiganians have already cast absentee ballots.

Trump in recent weeks has derisively called Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney "governor," labeled Canadian officials "nasty" and has complained that Canada is "one of the worst countries in the world to deal with," among other insults.

"They want to have a deal with us. They call us all the time. The problem is that they've treated the United States very unfairly," the Republican president told reporters in late September.

Republican Senate hopeful Rogers debuted the ad the day before he is set to face off in his first debate against Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed in Grand Rapids. The 30-second spot features Rogers wearing a flannel shirt and sitting at a bar stool at Bigg's Bar & Grill on Gratiot Avenue in Chesterfield Township.

More: Most Michigan voters oppose Trump tariffs on Canada, poll shows

A year ago, Rogers accused Democrats of "fear mongering" over Trump's tariffs, and said the president's tariff policy had "put the American people back in the driver's seat."

"President Trump is right to put America First, and tariffs are necessary when countries cheat American workers. But trade isn't one-size-fits-all," Rogers posted on social media on Aug. 29.

In an interview last month, Rogers again defended some of Trump's global tariffs and argued they had helped bring some manufacturing back to the U.S., pointing to General Motors Co.'s decision to move production of the Chevy Silverado pickup truck from Mexico to its Orion Township assembly plant.

Rogers did acknowledge that the tariffs against Canada are going to pinch Michigan consumers and said his team had conversations with the Trump administration about them.

"This is why you want to send somebody back (to Washington) who can have a conversation about what's working for Michigan and what might not work for Michigan, if you send somebody back that all they want to do is get on TikTok and talk about President Trump, we're not going to fix up one single problem," Rogers told The Detroit News.

"But if you send a guy like me back, we're going to have this conversation."

Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, by contrast, has frequently bashed Trump and Rogers over the ongoing trade war with Michigan's international neighbor, calling the Canadian tariffs "chaotic" and costly.

El-Sayed on Wednesday accused Rogers of flip-flopping again.

"Must have had one too many of those LaBatts, Mike. You cheerled this tariff war from the beginning and you're flip-flopping now because your poll numbers are in free fall," El-Sayed posted on X.com in response to Rogers' ad.

"Donald is the reason we're in a trade war. And he's the reason you're running. Not a serious person."

El-Sayed at an August campaign event said that Canadians "are the only people I know who will preemptively apologize for something they never did ... You gotta be an a------ to pick a trade war with Canada. I'm so sorry, like, they're like the nicest people on Earth."

A Detroit News/WDIV-TV (Channel 4) poll conducted just before Labor Day found that less than one-third (29%) of 600 likely general election voters in Michigan approve of Trump's decision to impose 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, including cement, wine, dairy and hockey sticks.

Nearly two-thirds (64%) said they disapprove, according to the survey conducted by the Lansing-based Glengariff Group polling firm Aug. 31 to Sept. 3. The poll has a margin of error of plus or minus four percentage points.

The overwhelming majority of Democratic (93%) and independent (73%) poll participants opposed the tariffs, while most Republicans support them — though there is division within the GOP. About 1 in 4 (24%) of base GOP voters disapprove.

"There is just wholesale opposition to these tariffs," pollster Richard Czuba said of the poll results. "And what really stands out to me is Michiganders understand the financial impact of these tariffs on them."

About 62% of respondents said Trump's tariffs on Canada are bad for Michigan's economy, with 17% saying the tariffs are good. That split is especially pronounced among independent voters, who tend to play a major role in who wins and loses in Michigan elections and 70% of whom said the Canadian tariffs are bad for the state's economy.

Nearly 72% of the likely Michigan voters said the Canadian tariffs would cause an increase in what they pay for goods, according to the poll results.

Some elected Republicans in Michigan have expressed a desire for the Trump administration and Canadian officials to resolve the trade conflict, but they have stopped short of criticizing the president directly.

Republican U.S. Rep. John James, who is running for governor, in an Oct. 6 debate said he's called the Trump administration, specifically talking with the trade ambassador "and saying that we must get back to the table, stop acting like children, and negotiate a reciprocal, fair, and mutually beneficial arrangement to make sure that we can bring our jobs back and protect our industry."

U.S. House hopeful Michael Bouchard of Rochester Hills, a Republican running for James' vacant 10th District seat, said he'd like to see Trump's tariffs on Canadian imports end.

"I don't think our trade conflict with Canada is where we should be focusing a lot of our effort," Bouchard said Oct. 7 in an interview on The Detroit News' Political Insider podcast. "Everybody in Michigan knows Canadians. They're friends with Canada. It's 30 minutes from here to Canada."

Bouchard distinguished his remarks on Canadian tariffs from his support for Trump's global tariffs against China and other countries that are needed to "make sure that Americans are put in a position to succeed.

"But this tariffs on Canada stuff, I've been pretty blunt about that from the beginning," Bouchard said.

GOP U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett of Charlotte, who is locked in a tough reelection fight in his mid-Michigan district, told CNN on Sept. 9 that he's advocating for "cooler heads to prevail" in what he called a "tit for tat" back-and-forth between the U.S. and Canada.

"I want to see us get to a point where we can have mutually beneficial trade arrangements with Canada," Barrett said.

"I'm still hopeful that we'll get there, but that has been my advocacy ― both publicly and behind the scenes ― so that we can move in that direction. And I think it's going to take movement by both sides, the United States and Canada, to get to a mutual arrangement."

The former state lawmaker suggested on CNN that tariffs should be narrowly tailored to balance "anomalies" within U.S. trade arrangements. Barrett pointed to Canada's long-standing tariffs on U.S. dairy products, a policy designed to protect its country's milk, cheese and butter producers from competition.

Barrett said dairy farmers in his district are struggling to make market margins "in no small part because Canada has really manipulated their market there."

U.S. Rep. John Moolenaar, a Caledonia Republican, said last month that he is hoping for an end to the ongoing U.S.-Canada trade dispute, calling some of the negotiations so far counterproductive.

"Unfortunately, what normally is a civil private negotiation working towards agreements has spilled into some name-calling and some things that haven't been as productive as I'd like," Moolenaar said during a telephone town hall on Sept. 1.

"Quite frankly, we've got some work ahead of us," Moolenaar added. "Canada is an important trading partner, and my goal is to see this resolved in a constructive way."

title: Trump wants to turn his West Palm Beach golf course into the new Camp David
description:
Much of President Donald Trump’s second term has focused on changes to the nation’s capital.
But his ambitions to remake the physical architecture of the presidency transcend Washington: Trump wants to transform his West Palm Beach golf club into a presidential retreat modeled after Camp David.
Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. 
The plan calls for a parcel of the private club to be designated a permanent, official sanctuary for foreign leaders and future U.S.
fullText:
Much of President Donald Trump's second term has focused on changes to the nation's capital.

But his ambitions to remake the physical architecture of the presidency transcend Washington: Trump wants to transform his West Palm Beach golf club into a presidential retreat modeled after Camp David.

The plan calls for a parcel of the private club to be designated a permanent, official sanctuary for foreign leaders and future U.S. presidents, designed to host international summits and house presidents when they take vacations in Florida, according to a proposal presented to Palm Beach County officials by Trump International Golf Club's legal counsel. Future presidents would also be offered comped memberships to the Trump club.

"Just as Camp David, Windsor Castle, or the Elysee Palace are known worldwide, so too will the Presidential Golf Course in Palm Beach County," Harvey Oyer, a lawyer representing the Trump course, wrote to the Palm Beach County Board of County Commissioners in a letter last month. Oyer asked the county, which owns the property the course is on, to provide a piece of the land to the federal government, and he promised Trump would pay for the construction of a presidential residence and facilities on that land.

Oyer told The Washington Post that a name has yet not been selected for the presidential golf course.

"It would further cement Palm Beach County as one of the most recognizable brands and destinations in the world," Oyer said.

A spokesperson for the Trump Organization did not respond to requests for comment.

A White House official with knowledge of the proposed plans said in a text message the facilities would provide amenities of a "world-class property."

"The property is minutes away from the Donald J. Trump International Airport, does not have buildings looming, does not have houses along the course, has great security features, is close to law enforcement, and happens to be a highly rated golf course. These are features that are necessary for any presidential retreat," said the White House official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to preview plans.

In the letter, which was first reported by the Palm Beach Post, Oyer said the construction would not be completed before Trump leaves office, so the project would be "a gift" to Trump's successors and the county would benefit from high-power traffic in the area.

The county is seriously considering the proposal and is seeking more information, Palm Beach County Administrator Joseph Abruzzo told The Washington Post. In a meeting last week, Trump representatives assured county officials that, under the proposal, Trump's company would continue to make lease payments for the golf course and would agree to build the presidential retreat on a connected piece of land that would have a separate entrance from the private club, Abruzzo said.

Trump's club would continue to operate under the Trump family company and would probably benefit from more business if it becomes a site of long-lasting presidential importance.

The county is in contact with the General Services Administration, the agency that manages federal properties, and the county will be selecting a parcel of the land for the proposal, Abruzzo said.

"My understanding is that President Trump views this as a lasting contribution to the presidency and to those who will hold the office after him," Abruzzo said.

Though presidents already have a retreat at Camp David, Trump has visited the complex less frequently than many of his predecessors, preferring to spend his weekends and holidays at his own properties. He once commented that Camp David's rustic charm would wear off after half an hour.

Previous presidents have left their own marks on the woodsy Maryland retreat. Franklin D. Roosevelt established the getaway for federal workers as a presidential compound and dubbed it Shangri-La, though Dwight D. Eisenhower later named it after his father and grandson.

Marjorie Merriweather Post, who was once the wealthiest woman in the United States, also had hoped to create a presidential retreat in the South. She gifted her Palm Beach estate - better known as Mar-a-Lago - to the federal government upon her death in 1973, with the intention that it be turned into a Winter White House. But the National Park Service returned the property to her estate due to high maintenance costs, and Trump bought the property in 1985.

Trump International Golf Club opened in 1999 after Trump settled a lawsuit with the county regarding airplanes flying over Mar-a-Lago and the county agreed to lend him the land. Near the golf course, state officials have branded the Palm Beach airport and the road along it with Trump's name.

Trump's influence over Palm Beach and its image would be further cemented if the golf club becomes a presidential retreat. The wealthy strip of South Florida has undergone a MAGA transformation with Trump's base flocking to Mar-a-Lago for political events and networking. The nearby golf club has become a go-to destination for Trump spotting.

Trump reported an income of nearly $37 million last year from the golf course in his latest financial disclosure.

Although Trump had mocked former president Barack Obama for golfing during his presidency, Trump has frequently golfed since he has been in office. One online tracker calculated that Trump has spent at least 137 days in his second term golfing.

Rick Reilly, a former Sports Illustrated columnist who wrote "Commander in Cheat: How Golf Explains Trump," has golfed with Trump and said the president is less interested in the sport than the attention he gains at his own clubs. Reilly described how Trump always plays first in his golfing party and speeds on his golf cart to the next hole, wrapping up his game in less time than is typical, before heading to the clubhouse, where he makes the rounds, talking to his members and fans. If the Palm Beach club were a destination for foreign leaders, they would be part of the display of influence.

"I suppose he wants to make a power play with these people and show them who is the king of America," Reilly said.

Don Van Natta Jr., an ESPN senior writer who wrote "First Off the Tee: Presidential Hackers, Duffers, and Cheaters From Taft to Bush," a book on the history of presidents who golfed, said 17 of the past 20 presidents have golfed. The first avid golfer in the Oval Office was William Howard Taft, and the last president who didn't golf was Jimmy Carter.

"There is a long history of presidents playing golf," Van Natta said. "It's an escape where they can, as President [Bill] Clinton told me for my book, to be out in nature, and it's an escape hatch from the pressures of the Oval Office."

CORRECTION: A photo caption with a previous version of this article and on the homepage omitted the year that President Donald Trump arrived at Trump International Golf Club to watch the Super Bowl. It was in 2017.

title: Washington resident accused of helping plan Canada's Tumbler Ridge school shooting
description:
People pay their respects at a memorial on the steps of the Town Hall, following a vigil the previous day, in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, Canada, Feb. 14, 2026. - Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press/AP
US authorities have announced the arrest of a 30-year-old from Washington state in connection with the February school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia.
The person, identified by authorities as James Cody Bryant, was arrested in Bellingham, Washington, on Tuesday morning on a charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country, according to an announcement by the US Justice Department. The February attack on a secondary school in the small town of Tumbler Ridge was Canada’s deadliest school shooting in decades, leaving eight people dead, including six children, and dozens wounded.
fullText:
US authorities have arrested a 30-year-old from Washington state in connection with the February school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia.

James Cody Bryant was arrested in Bellingham, Washington, on Tuesday morning on a charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country, according to the US Justice Department. The February attack on a secondary school in the small town at the foothills of the Rocky Mountains was Canada’s deadliest school shooting in decades, leaving eight people dead, including six children, and dozens wounded.

Bryant appeared in court Tuesday afternoon in Seattle. CNN has reached out to Bryant’s lawyer for comment. A hearing has been set for October 20.

Bryant was allegedly “in repeated contact with” the 18-year-old Canadian shooter, Jesse Van Rootselaar, “offering advice, sending money and even agreeing to live stream the horrific event” on Twitch, said Neil Floyd, the acting US attorney for the Western District of Washington, at a press conference in Seattle.

The money Bryant gave the shooter amounted to a little over $100, primarily to buy a lighter and a pair of shoes that Van Rootselaar “wanted to have when she conducted this killing spree,” Floyd said. The two discussed sending weapons to Van Rootselaar, but Bryant was uncomfortable with doing so and refused, according to a complaint filed in court on Friday.

Bryant began an online friendship with Van Rootselaar after meeting on video chatting website Omegle three years before the shooting, authorities said. An affidavit within the complaint includes excerpts of chat logs between Bryant and Van Rootselaar on the Discord website.

“I read a lot of court documents, including some that discuss incredibly heinous acts of violence, but this complaint was particularly difficult to read,” said FBI agent Mike Harrington at the Tuesday press conference, “in part because of the casual tone these two individuals used when discussing the mass taking of innocent lives that was being planned.”

In one exchange, Van Rootselaar allegedly told Bryant that she wanted to “avoid doing a school” but that “there’s just so many reasons why it’s ideal.” According to the affidavit, Bryant responded in turn that attacking a hotel “seems like a good idea.”

After Van Rootselaar killed two family members, Bryant allegedly offered the attacker advice on how to fix a car when it failed to start en route to the school.

Canadian and US authorities have said that Bryant and Van Rootselaar, who died in the shooting, are trans women, though officials used male and female pronouns interchangeably to describe the two throughout the press conference.

Assistant Commissioner Elija Rain of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police said Canadian authorities contacted the US Department of Homeland Security soon after the shooting, based on “information from one of the online platforms used by the shooter.”

“As further alleged, instead of de-escalating or reporting to law enforcement, Bryant continued to enable the shooter over the months they discussed these plans,” said Harrington. “In addition to providing money, technical advice and particular items to be used in the shooting, Bryant agreed to record a live stream feed of the attack and broadcast it in a way that would maximize notoriety for the shooter.”

It was not previously known that anyone apart from Van Rootselaar allegedly participated in planning the massacre. CNN previously reported Van Rootselaar posted about guns and hunting and her apparent mental health struggles online in the lead up to the massacre.

Seven families of victims sued tech company OpenAI in April after information emerged that the shooter had used ChatGPT to plan the attack. The week before the suit was filed, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman apologized to the community for not alerting law enforcement after Van Rootselaar’s account was banned.

CNN’s Josh Campbell, Paula Newton and Lex Harvey contributed reporting. This story has been updated with additional developments.

title: Trump makes it clear his power is becoming entwined with AI
description:

New alliances between the White House, the Pentagon, US intelligence and AI companies are looming ominously

Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, writing to you as I sit under yellowing leaves in New York. Today in tech, we’re discussing technocracy.

Donald Trump made a series of moves over the past week that make it clear his power is becoming synonymous with artificial intelligence.

The new tight alliances between the White House, the Pentagon, US intelligence agencies and AI companies loom ominously over governments and companies, particularly in Europe, that rely on American AI.

Last Tuesday, Trump and six AI CEOs signed what he called a “morally binding” agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence. The vague agreement stipulates a framework for what Trump called “tremendous self-policing”, reiterating his point that AI companies can act as their own watchmen. Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Jensen Huang and Dario Amodei signed.

Zuckerberg hand-guided the writing of that agreement, Semafor reported. The pact reportedly arose from a conversation between the Meta CEO and House speaker, Mike Johnson, at the US state dinner for Xi Jinping, which preceded the conclave of the tech CEOs. Zuckerberg circulated a draft of the agreement in advance of the convening, and Huang threw his support behind it, per Semafor.

It is one thing for tech executives to dine at the White House to curry favor with the president; it is entirely another to have them draft the terms of executive orders. Silicon Valley’s CEOs are writing contracts that bear the White House letterhead, entrenching their interests and their power.

“It’s almost like a constitution in a way, and the biggest ​people in the world signed that, and ​I signed it as president, and it really ⁠is a form of protection,” Trump said. Famously, constitutions are legally binding, which Zuckerberg and Trump’s agreement is not.

The president also decreed that government documents render any reference to “artificial intelligence” as “super intelligence”. How loyal will they be to his rebrand?

At least one acquiesced immediately: Musk copied the renaming by changing the name of one of his company’s subsidiaries from SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI. The change coincided with the multi-CEO’s re-entry into government work more than a year after his explosive term at Doge ended. On Thursday, the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, named Musk to a taskforce to study the future of warfare alongside Palmer Luckey and Emil Michael, dubbed Project Meridian. The trio of men will release a report in 120 days with public recommendations on how to achieve “absolute technological dominance on the next-generation battlefield”, in the words of Hegseth.

Over the weekend, the president announced that he had appointed Jay Clayton, director of national intelligence, as the AI czar of his administration.

Trump’s first AI czar was a Silicon Valley insider. David Sacks is a venture capitalist who championed growth and deregulation during his term as a special government employee. He maintained direct financial stakes in multiple AI companies while working with the White House, indicating his ultimate goal was to build a bigger fortune. (He’s made a name for himself recently championing AI accelerationism, the opposing philosophical camp to the “doomerism” of the Anthropic employees who prophesy extinction.)

The second czar, Clayton, is the leader of the US’s spy agencies, a job he will continue to hold in addition to overseeing AI initiatives. His joint appointment sends a very different message, one echoed by Hegseth: AI will supercharge the offensive capabilities of the US government, in particular surveillance and the gathering of intel. Clayton’s ascendancy has major worldwide implications: US spying agencies dictating global AI policy does not bode well for the sovereignty of other nations that need cutting-edge AI.

The US economy is already extremely dependent on the growth of the artificial intelligence sector. The companies whose leaders attended Trump’s summit are responsible for the majority of the US stock market’s growth over the past five years.

The latest moves by Trump’s administration signal that American power is likewise inextricable from AI, synonymous: executive authority, military might and the government’s information. The White House pledge binds Trump and the AI CEOs together; Hegseth’s taskforce ties the Pentagon to Musk and Luckey’s visions of automated war in space; and making Clayton the AI czar predicts an era of AI-enabled spying, of government knowledge being gathered and filtered through large language models.

One point of striking divergence: labor. The economy writ large may rest on AI, but the workers of the US do not. The majority of the hiring happening in the US is not a result of AI companies’ growth, according to the US jobs report released on Friday. Far more people are being hired to work in healthcare, a sector that still needs human labor more than automated work. AI may fuel gross domestic product growth, but it is not driving job creation on a national scale.

title: Trump allies push to sideline AI safety advocates as fight over oversight grows
description:
BERKELEY, Calif. - After artificial intelligence safety advocates captured Washington’s attention with dire warnings about the technology’s power, the Trump administration and its allies embraced some of their suggestions, while moving to sideline the advocates themselves.
Battle lines have been drawn in recent days over part of an accord signed by President Donald Trump and AI chief executives last week: Who should audit AI companies’ systems to ensure their technology behaves as intended. 
Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. 
Leading AI companies - including OpenAI and Anthropic - have for years worked with a cluster of nonprofits concentrated in the Bay Area’s AI safety community, which grew out of the effective altruism movement.
fullText:
BERKELEY, Calif. - After artificial intelligence safety advocates captured Washington's attention with dire warnings about the technology's power, the Trump administration and its allies embraced some of their suggestions, while moving to sideline the advocates themselves.

Battle lines have been drawn in recent days over part of an accord signed by President Donald Trump and AI chief executives last week: Who should audit AI companies' systems to ensure their technology behaves as intended.

Leading AI companies - including OpenAI and Anthropic - have for years worked with a cluster of nonprofits concentrated in the Bay Area's AI safety community, which grew out of the effective altruism movement. But Trump's tech-world allies say the work of auditing AI should be taken on by America's largest consulting firms.

"In my view they should be professional auditors, not these NGOs," investor and former top White House AI adviser David Sacks said on his All-In podcast last week. He said in a post on X last month that the AI safety nonprofit METR, which has worked with Anthropic, was too close to the company to be called independent. Soon after, Anthropic said it would partner with consulting giant Accenture to build a team of outside evaluators.

At a conference here over the weekend, members of AI safety organizations grappled with the impact of what some see as a coordinated campaign to delegitimize their work and paint their community as cultish and unserious. The event took place at a former hotel popular with AI safety acolytes that also recently hosted a conference on AI consciousness and a sex workshop called "Slutcon."

Trump officials and allies have sniped at the movement for months but the attacks intensified after public anxiety over AI risks forced the White House to respond. Sacks last month shared on X a New York Post front page that called employees of METR, which helped OpenAI investigate its rogue AI agents, "THE WOKE WIZARDS OF AI." (The Washington Post has a content partnership with OpenAI.)

Trump on Sunday named several figures who have rejected calls from advocates for an AI industry-wide slowdown to his Super Intelligence Force advisory panel. They include Sacks and Emil Michael, the Pentagon's chief technology officer, who said last month that calls for action to prevent extreme scenarios of AI causing harm promoted "extinction, death-cult-like philosophies."

"There has absolutely been a rhetorical push within certain corners of the White House and broader Trump administration to get the message out about effective altruism and its potential dangers," said a Trump administration official, speaking on the condition of anonymity to describe private discussions.

A White House official said that it supports organizations that evaluate the security and safety of how AI models are engineered. The official pointed to Trump's 2025 executive order targeting what the president termed "woke AI."

Nathan Leamer, director of the pro-industry nonprofit Build American AI, said he has been briefing congressional staff and other influential conservative figures in Washington about effective altruism, describing it as antithetical to his own Christian values.

"A year ago no one in Hill offices knew what effective altruism was," Leamer said. Build American AI is linked to Leading the Future, a political campaign group funded by the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz and OpenAI President Greg Brockman, a major midterms Republican donor.

Brad Carson, co-founder of Americans for Responsible Innovation, which says it is focused on AI policy in the public interest, said that Trump allies are trying discredit anyone pushing for meaningful AI regulation, an idea that now has significant momentum.

"In D.C., at least, and maybe in the broader culture, we won that fight. The vibe is with us," said Carson, who also leads a political advocacy organization funded in part by Anthropic. "People are very concerned. Congress wants to regulate."

But leaders of AI evaluation start-ups that did not grow out of the AI safety movement said some Washington Republicans are distrustful of the label.

"It almost felt like a new version of McCarthyism," said Rayan Krishnan, CEO of the Andreessen Horowitz-backed start-up Vals AI, after a trip to Washington last month to pitch his start-up to the public sector.

Judd Rosenblatt, CEO of AE Studio, who described himself as a conservative small business owner, said multiple people in the Trump administration have told his team that they see the need for third parties to assess AI tools, but are wary of effective altruism, he said.

Civil society groups that have been auditing AI systems since before the debut of ChatGPT warn there is a risk that an opportunity for oversight of opaque AI giants will be squandered.

"Where we find ourselves now is trying to determine who will actually be in the room in making decisions," said Miranda Bogen, chief technologist at the Center for Democracy & Technology and director of the advocacy group's AI Governance Lab, one of various groups eager to contribute their expertise in standard-setting.

The accord signed by AI chief executives last week, which Trump called "morally binding," was frequently mentioned onstage and in huddles between sessions at the Berkeley conference last weekend, where attendees endured a heat wave with fans and Popsicles.

At a Sunday discussion panel on what the AI auditor ecosystem might look like, one speaker said they are working on building a broad coalition of experts, including people working on bias and discrimination as well as blue-chip firms like Accenture and Deloitte. Panelists also discussed other ways the community could prove its legitimacy. Another suggested two-month boot camps to train a talent pipeline of qualified auditors.

Adam Gleave, CEO of FAR.AI, a nonprofit research institute, said in an interview that excluding the AI safety community would shut out people with expertise that are important in the current moment.

"When it comes to looking at millions of agent transcripts and trying to piece together what they did and how they were interacting, I don't think there are many organizations in the world that have that expertise," Gleave said. "The reality is that anyone you hire with that background is going to have some connection to the industry."

On his podcast, Sacks and his co-hosts, who remain close to the White House, made clear that they preferred instead to have established corporate giants do the work.

"You're going to see EY in short order here announce something," said investor Chamath Palihapitiya, who earlier in the episode said his start-up 8090 was building the global accounting firm formerly known as Ernst & Young "an entire audit infrastructure for super intelligence," and that 8090 now plans to "roll it out to everybody."

EY said in a statement that it was working with 8090 to "develop new capabilities that bring greater visibility, traceability and human accountability to consequential AI-enabled decisions and workflows."

title: Justice Samuel Alito says same-sex marriage ruling marked a turn against religious liberty
description:
Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito, the devout Catholic conservative who has long warned of animus against religion in America, says in a new book that he believes the court's landmark decision extending marriage rights to same-sex couples was "perhaps the decisive point in our nation's turn against religious liberty."
Alito, who dissented sharply in the 2015 case, made the claim at Catholic University of America three years after Obergefell v Hodges in a speech that was not open to the public or widely covered at the time. The remarks were published this month in "So Ordered," a collection of Alito speeches that he says reflect his judicial philosophy and outlook on the country.
J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo - PHOTO: Associate Justice Samuel Alito stands in his chambers at the Supreme Court during an Associated Press interview, in Washington, Sept.
fullText:
In a new book, the Supreme Court justice reflects on his "pet issue" of faith.

Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito, the devout Catholic conservative who has long warned of animus against religion in America, says in a new book that he believes the court's landmark decision extending marriage rights to same-sex couples was "perhaps the decisive point in our nation's turn against religious liberty."

Alito, who dissented sharply in the 2015 case, made the claim at Catholic University of America three years after Obergefell v Hodges in a speech that was not open to the public or widely covered at the time. The remarks were published this month in "So Ordered," a collection of Alito speeches that he says reflect his judicial philosophy and outlook on the country.

Seven of the 19 Alito speeches published in the book were delivered to Catholic groups.

"In dissent from that ruling," he said in the 2018 address, "I expressed my worry that equating the expression of certain views with bigotry -- or, if you like, with dignitary harm -- would drive believers out of public life."

Alito suggests that his prediction has come to pass.

"Quite suddenly, religious liberty has become controversial," Alito said in a newly published 2022 speech to the Magnificat Foundation, a nonprofit group dedicated to promoting Catholic culture and traditions.

Throughout the book, the justice cites a string of lawsuits to reach the Supreme Court in recent years as evidence that, in his opinion, "support for religious liberty has cratered."

The cases he uses as examples involve businesses threatened with punishment for refusing to provide services for gay weddings and faith-based organizations harmed by government health or employment regulations without any religious exemption.

"What we see in these and other cases," Alito says in the 2022 speech, "is a refusal to live in peace with those who violate the new moral code." He says the dynamic will "virtually guarantee that the Supreme Court will continue to see a steady stream of religious-liberty cases."

In nearly all the cases Alito cites as examples of religious animus, the court ultimately sided with the religiously affiliated parties over their opponents.

The court ruled in favor of a Colorado baker who was sued for refusing to create a wedding cake for a gay couple and later defended a Christian wedding website designer who objected to creating sites for same-sex ceremonies.

When the Affordable Care Act mandated that employers provide insurance plans with no-cost contraceptive coverage, the high court ruled that some private employers can opt-out as a matter of faith and that federal agencies must be allowed to exempt religious employers from the rule.

The court recently ruled that states must allow religiously affiliated private schools to participate in state-funded private tuition programs and tax credit initiatives. Last year, it gave parents the right to opt-out their kids from teachings that conflict with sincere religious beliefs.

The conservative majority blocked a bid by the city of Philadelphia to exclude Catholic Social Services from its foster care program over LGBT discrimination and later effectively struck down state laws banning LGBT conversion therapy, which some religious advocates said amounted to a gag order against Christian teaching about human sexuality.

Recent decisions have also expanded protection for religious exercise on the job -- siding with a former public school football coach who had been disciplined for praying at midfield after games -- and mandated broader employer accommodations for the faithful who need to skip work to attend worship services.

Alito joined the majority in all of those cases and has voted in favor of faith-based interests in many others over his 20 years on the high court.

The issue of same-sex marriage rights, which was narrowly decided 5-4, remains a flashpoint.

Many LGBTQ advocates have begun to fear, in part from public criticism aired by Justice Alito, that Obergefell may not be on settled ground.

In 2025, Alito said publicly that while he strongly opposes the ruling, he is "not suggesting that the decision should be overruled," even as fellow conservative Justice Clarence Thomas has openly urged his colleagues to do so.

Nevertheless, Alito suggests in his book that the marriage decision has effectively silenced Americans whose sincere religious beliefs favor limiting unions to one man and one woman, likening them to Catholics who were sidelined in post-Reformation England.

They "had been so beaten down that they were 'a people who shunned the light of day.' They were 'found in corners, and alleys, and cellars, and the housetops, or in the recesses of the country,'" he said in a newly-published speech delivered in 2021 at Thomas Aquinas College.

"What I predicted in my dissent is coming to pass," Alito said of same-sex marriage opponents.

While many religious liberty advocates openly share Alito's concerns, some have voiced a different view of the current state of affairs.

"We continue to win unparalleled court victories at every level of the judiciary furthering the religious liberty of all Americans, resulting in more religious freedom today than at any other time in our lives," wrote Jeff Mateer, executive vice president and chief operating and legal officer of First Liberty Institute in the group's 2025 annual report. The nonprofit group calls itself the "nation's largest legal advocacy firm dedicated to defending religious liberty" and frequently brings cases to the high court.

The Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, another high profile nonprofit religious advocacy group, says in its 2025 report on religious freedom in America that "faith in the public square is on the rise." "Americans are moving away from a timid, behind-closed-doors view of religious freedom," Becket found.

One of six Catholic justices on the current court, Alito, who calls freedom of religion a "pet issue," concedes the legal victories for religious exercise rights but maintains a critical view of threats to people of faith.

"It says a lot that the parties whose free-exercise rights were violated had to take their claims all the way to our Court," he said at the 2021 event.

The book also highlights the justice's views on originalism and textualism; the role of judges in American life; and what he calls "threats" to the Constitution.

fullText:
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration pushed the FBI to investigate Los Angeles protesters in violation of their constitutional rights and the bureau’s policies, a former FBI supervisor alleges in a new whistleblower complaint.

Jill Fields, a former supervisory intelligence analyst in the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, made a formal whistleblower complaint to Senate Judiciary Committee leaders over the federal response to anti-ICE protest activity around federal buildings, as well as in a residential area, early last year.

Fields asked Congress and the Justice Department’s watchdog to investigate the allegations, her attorneys said in a letter to lawmakers. She says they violated the First Amendment right to free speech and to peaceably assemble.

Fields says Emil Bove, then the acting deputy attorney general, told the head of the field office to open an investigation into activities outside the federal building even though, she says, the activities were protected free speech. Separately, she says the White House gave a directive to FBI Director Kash Patel to investigate a group of protesters using megaphones during immigration enforcement operations after FBI agents had conducted a check into the conduct and declined to open an investigation.

President Donald Trump had viewed a video of people using megaphones to alert residents about immigration activities, advise them of their legal rights and encourage them not to open their doors unless immigration enforcement agents had signed judicial warrants, according to the letter.

A person whose name is redacted in the complaint told Fields that an investigation would be opened because “the President wants this investigation,” Fields’ whistleblower complaint says.

The protests were staged across Los Angeles after the Trump administration launched an immigration enforcement operation. Fields said the FBI’s Los Angeles office had pulled agents off active cartel cases to satisfy what a supervisor described as “optics” designed to “make a show for the president.” The area would be the scene of major protests later in the year during an immigration surge in cities nationwide.

A Justice Department spokesperson called the whistleblower complaint politically-motivated and said that violence is not protected by the First Amendment, though the complaint focused on non-violent protests.

“Under President Trump, the Department of Justice will continue to vigorously uphold the First Amendment rights of all Americans and restore the rule of law,” the spokesperson said. “The DOJ and FBI have a responsibility to investigate any potential violations of federal law, and conspiracies to impede federal law enforcement and assaults on federal officers are against the law.”

The FBI didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Justice Department officials have previously said government workers need to follow the Trump administration’s priorities. Last week, Justice Department leaders filed an administrative complaint about federal judges who made remarks to the media about the impact the surge in immigration enforcement had on their courtrooms.

Fields says supervisors were told not to put things in writing, so many of the directives came in face-to-face meetings. She says she didn’t know whether any formal investigation was opened because she was excluded once she refused to participate.

Fields consulted with a senior FBI official in charge of privacy and civil liberties matters, who expressed dismay about the investigation and subsequently told Fields she planned to resign, according to the complaint.

Fields, too, resigned from the bureau, after she was informed that she would be removed from heading three programs, a decision she believes constituted retaliation for making protected internal disclosures. The FBI’s actions, according to the letter, “created a chilling effect within the workforce” and “signaled to other employees that raising constitutional or legal concerns could carry professional consequences.”

The conduct “had significant consequences for constitutional rights, and the integrity and effective operation of the FBI,” according to the complaint.

Hundreds of FBI agents and Justice Department attorneys have resigned or been fired since Trump returned to office, particularly those who were involved in investigating him, and former Justice Department employees have expressed concerns that the nation’s top law enforcement agency is doing the bidding of the president.

Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., told NBC News that Fields’ disclosure is another instance of Trump’s weaponizing the Justice Department to go after his perceived political enemies. Padilla, who himself was forcibly removed from a news conference featuring then-Homeland Security Kristi Noem in June 2025, is the ranking member of the Judiciary subcommittee on immigration, citizenship and border safety.

“How many more of these investigations have been opened up because of political pressure coming from the White House, despite the questions and concerns about legality and constitutionality?” Padilla said.

He acknowledged that the Trump administration’s attacks on civil service protections through unilateral firings, as well as the mass firings of internal government watchdogs, had an impact on the legislative branch’s ability to conduct oversight.

“That’s going to be a significant challenge, but it begins with good, honorable professionals being willing to come forward and tell us what’s going on and what’s wrong with what’s going on,” Padilla said. “We’re hoping others may be inspired, as well.”

In a letter Padilla sent to Attorney General Todd Blanche and Patel, Padilla wrote that the allegations in the Fields disclosure “raise grave concerns about the rule of law under your leadership, the diversion of resources from ongoing criminal investigations, and the testimony that you provided under oath to Congress.”

The senator asked for officials to preserve information about the investigation and send any details to his office.

Fields was represented by the nonprofit Government Accountability Project and David Laufman, a former top official in the Justice Department’s National Security Section.

title: Russia disputes plague report as Trump offers U.S. help
description:

fullText:
Russia on Monday sought to downplay reports that a laboratory technician had died of plague, even as President Donald Trump said Washington was closely monitoring the situation and offered US help.

Reports on Friday that pneumonic plague had killed a 28-year-old woman named Darya Shipilova, who had been working for the anti-plague institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region, sparked alarm.

"We're looking at it very strongly, we just heard about it," Trump told reporters at the White House when asked what Washington was going to do about the risk of plague coming from Russia.

"We'll help them, we'll help them as much as we can."

The Russian news outlet People of Baikal, citing unnamed sources close to the regional security services, said the dead woman may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube.

Other media reported a possible link between her death and a lab accident at the facility.

As many as 200 people with whom she may have had contact were under quarantine, the People of Baikal outlet added, without elaborating.

But Russian officials stressed that postmortem tests had not detected the disease.

Irkutsk Regional Governor Igor Kobzev said Monday that a special expert commission inspection in the region had found that "the cause of death was pneumonia of undetermined aetiology".

He said on Telegram that Russia's consumer and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor had determined, following tests, that "no microorganisms linked to the young woman's professional work were found in her biological samples".

He added that there had been "no new cases of staff from the anti-plague institute seeking medical attention" since the woman's death.

Kobzev said the sanitary-epidemiological situation in Irkutsk was "stable".

"The situation remains under our control and that of the experts."

Asked about the situation on Monday, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters to "rely on Rospotrebnadzor's official statements rather than... rumours and speculations".

Plague is a bacterial disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, which is the most contagious type and can be transmitted by respiratory means. Bubonic plague is transmitted by infected fleas.

Pneumonic plague can be fatal if not treated early, according to the World Health Organization.

The reports will be closely watched in Washington, where memories of the Covid-19 pandemic that started in Trump's first term are still fresh.

Trump has strongly backed the theory that the disease was due to a leak from a laboratory in Wuhan, China.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said his country was monitoring the Russia situation but saw no "cause for alarm".

"There's very limited travel between the US and Russia, obviously, but like anything else, something like that gets out, it could quickly spread," Rubio told reporters before taking off for a visit to Iceland.

"So we're watching and monitoring it closely. I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on it. And we're doing that."

Experts said the reported response in Russia appeared "proportionate".

"It appears that measures are being implemented to quarantine any potential contacts and prevent any onward transmission," Malick Gibani, clinical associate professor in bacterial vaccinology, Imperial College London, said in a commentary.

title: Washington Wizards 2026-27 Preseason Preview
description: The Washington Wizards are entering a new era. After starting the rebuild process in 2023, the Wizards threw themselves into the deep end and lost…a lot. They dropped at least 64 games for three straight seasons and won just 17 in 2025-26. But through the dark years, Washington has gained young talent, the No. 1 […] The post Washington Wizards 2026-27 Preseason Preview appeared first on The Lead.
fullText:
The Washington Wizards are entering a new era. After starting the rebuild process in 2023, the Wizards threw themselves into the deep end and lost…a lot. They dropped at least 64 games for three straight seasons and won just 17 in 2025-26. But through the dark years, Washington has gained young talent, the No. 1 pick, and stars for cheap.

It acquired Trae Young for CJ McCollum and Corey Kispert a month before the trade deadline. The next month, Washington brought home Anthony Davis and others for Khris Middleton, AJ Johnson, Malaki Branham, Marvin Bagley III, and draft capital. Young played five games in Wizards colors, while Davis is yet to suit up.

The Wizards used their first No. 1 overall selection since 2010 on AJ Dybantsa. The BYU forward led the nation in scoring and did it through unique athleticism and jump shooting. They also used the offseason to bring in some complementary pieces to add more depth to the roster.

Last season wasn't pretty, but the pieces are in place to ascend and leave the reconstruction chapter; 2026-27 will answer if playoff basketball returns to the capital.

30 teams in 30 days: Washington Wizards pic.twitter.com/FUvFzPCIE2

— Underdog NBA (@UnderdogNBA) September 24, 2026

Washington traded Cam Whitmore to the Cleveland Cavaliers and received Tre Mann and a 2027 second-round pick in August. Whitmore's departure being the biggest hit to the Wizards' roster says something.

He played just 21 games off the bench for Washington as he was limited by a blood clot injury in his right shoulder. In Whitmore's 16.9 minutes on the floor, he averaged 9.2 points per game on 45.6% shooting — solid production. But in a depth chart with Dybantsa, Bilal Coulibaly, Will Riley, and Kyshawn George ahead of him, Whitmore wasn't going to be utilized. Cleveland waived him and Denver picked him up.

The move wasn't extremely popular among Wizards fans. Mann played just 66 games in the last two seasons. Last year, he competed for 12.6 minutes per contest and shot an unideal 36% from the field. He has shown flashes of potential, like his 14 points per game for Charlotte in 2024-25, albeit in just 14 appearances.

Losing Whitmore for Mann and a second-rounder may not have been a step forward, but it may not be a step back either, depicting how positive Washington's summer was.

— Hoop Central (@TheHoopCentral) December 2, 2025

Questions surrounded who Washington would select at No. 1 this June. While it wasn't clear who would have their name called, there was no doubt they'd be a generational talent. That's exactly what Dybantsa is.

Washington may be starting the beginning of a historic chapter in the franchise's history from day one of Dybantsa's career because of his sheer talent. The forward averaged 25.5 points per game on 51% shooting in his lone year as a Cougar.

His playstyle drew scouts' and fans' attention for a reason. Dybantsa can break down his defender on the perimeter with a hesitation or crossover, then choose his options from there: beat his next man with a sidestep to the lane, or fool him with a pivot and fadeaway jumper.

He scored at least 30 points eight times, two of which he scored at least 40. His 40 against Kansas State broke Kevin Durant's Big 12 Tournament freshman single-game scoring record. Dybantsa took the acclaim to the league, where he scored 27 points in his Summer League debut. That tied the most ever by a No. 1 pick.

He has the frame and athleticism of the all-time great scorers and is projected to rise near that level.

Dybantsa could win Rookie of the Year this season, which says a lot with the class he's competing with. First-year players of his caliber come in and change things in an instant, often making their team look brand new.

He doesn't just benefit Washington in 2027, but for years to come.

AJ Dybantsa Summer League Tape — 2 games pic.twitter.com/jRxCt4PQBT

— Basketball Performances (@NBAPerformances) July 22, 2026

Washington is an unproven team that looks incredible on paper. It has phenomenal pieces, but they've never been laid out on the board together. Can they fit to solve the puzzle that is the Wizards? The best-case scenario assumes they all do.

That means both chemistry and individual performance fall in line. It could look like Trae Young blending with Alex Sarr and Davis in the pick-and-roll while returning to efficient jump shooting. Or Davis' spacing working with Sarr's and keeping healthy. Even Dybantsa being able to contribute ROTY figures while Young and Tre Johnson still put up shots.

What follows is the quieter Wiz-Kids finally putting it together: Bub Carrington learns how to drive and defend, Coulibaly finds his shot, and Will Riley unlocks his brewing potential. Lastly, head coach Brian Keefe substantiates his position at the helm of the Wizards. The only years he's coached, Washington aimed to fail in. A productive season shows he has the answers to his first real test.

If all bodes well, Washington makes the playoffs for the first time in six years, and its ceiling is as high as the fifth seed. The Wizards could upset the fourth seed in a grinded-out seven games, barely coming out alive to advance for the first time since 2017. In the end, Washington falls to the powerhouse first seed in four or five games, proving it's made progress but has a ways to go.

For everything to go wrong, the Wizards' assortment of aging stars and untried youngsters must wither under raised expectations and fail to mix.

Young would have to get banged up, something he's not unfamiliar with, and contribute empty stats that look pretty but don't change results. Davis suffers an injury that sidelines him more than half the season, and his limited time on the court reflects a shell of himself from years ago.

Sarr hits a slump after a productive jump the year before, dropping his efficiency and stalling more defensive growth. Dybantsa looks like an overestimation, struggling to score anywhere outside the restricted area while Darryn Peterson and Cameron Boozer thrive.

With names piled on the injury list and promising prospects turned long-term projects, Washington drops to the 14th seed, just one place above its standing last year. It gets unluckier when, under the NBA's new draft lottery system, it is awarded the No. 12 pick in the draft following a poor year of trial and error.

While neither hypothetical is likely to be realized, there is one common thread that makes them possible: Anthony Davis' health. Can the 33-year-old, who has played a total of 71 games in the past two seasons, stay on the court?

It's hard to deny his production when active, even with the accumulated physical toll on his body through the years. Teams are better on both sides of the floor when he's on it because of his All-NBA caliber talent. But how regularly will he lace up his game-day shoes?

Davis is the key to the Wizards' 2026-27 season success.
