title: Trump says he’d consider pardoning members of his administration
description:
President Donald Trump said in an interview out Thursday that he would be open to pardoning members of his administration, pointing to former President Joe Biden’s blanket pardon to relatives and members of the administration out of concern they would be politically targeted after he left office. 
"Yeah, sure, I'd do that," the president answered when asked by TIME magazine earlier this week if he was "considering pardoning members of your administration prior to the end of your term?"
The president further said that Biden "gave pardons to everyone."
Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: President Donald Trump answers questions from reporters during an announcement in the Oval Office at the White House, September 28, 2026 in Washington.
Biden issued preemptive pardons to several close family members in the final minutes of his presidency in 2025, saying that his family "has been subjected to unrelenting attacks and threats, motivated solely by a desire to hurt me" and that he had "no reason to believe these attacks will end" after he left office.
fullText:
Trump defended such a move, saying Biden "gave pardons to everyone."

President Donald Trump said in an interview out Thursday that he would be open to pardoning members of his administration, pointing to former President Joe Biden’s blanket pardon to relatives and members of the administration out of concern they would be politically targeted after he left office.

"Yeah, sure, I'd do that," the president answered when asked by TIME magazine earlier this week if he was "considering pardoning members of your administration prior to the end of your term?"

The president further said that Biden "gave pardons to everyone."

Biden issued preemptive pardons to several close family members in the final minutes of his presidency in 2025, saying that his family "has been subjected to unrelenting attacks and threats, motivated solely by a desire to hurt me" and that he had "no reason to believe these attacks will end" after he left office.

Those pardons included James Biden, Joe's younger brother; Sara Jones Biden, James' wife; Valerie Biden Owens, Joe's younger sister; John T. Owens', Valerie's husband; and Francis W. Biden, Joe's younger brother.

In 2024, Biden pardoned his son, Hunter Biden, who was convicted on tax evasion and federal gun charges.

Trump's pardon comments mark the first time he has publicly said he would consider pardoning members of his administration.

Last year, he issued pardons to some to his political and financial supporters as well as several high-profile individuals allegedly involved in his attempt to overturn the election. In his first term, he pardoned several advisers, members of his campaign and one former member of his administration, former National Security Advisor Michael Flynn.

In the interview, Trump expressed his belief that if the Democrats emerge victorious in the midterm elections, “they'll probably go after" him, but he said he will also target them back.

Trump still expressed confidence that Republicans will "do okay" in November, as long as he is on the campaign trail.

"No, I think we'll do okay if I campaign, and I intend to," he said, when asked if he believes that Democrats will take control of Congress.

He then went on to tout some of his endorsement victories including for Republicans Darline Graham and Ed Gallerin -- who defeated Rep. Thomas Massie in the primary for Kentucky’s 4th Congressional District.

Asked about his record low poll numbers, Trump called them "fake" and insisted that he could easily beat anybody who ran against him.

"They're fake numbers. I would beat anybody running today by 20 points," Trump said. "Your numbers that you have are fake."

Trump's cover of TIME magazine will mark his 56th such appearance, according to the outlet. That's more than any other figure in history, surpassing former President Richard Nixon's record.

Trump's interview will be the cover story for TIME's Oct. 26 issue.

title: Bills react to tough start for Patriots QB Drake Maye
description: Buffalo Bills DC Jim Leonhard, New England Patriots QB Drake Maye on division matchup
fullText:
The Bills open division play Sunday against a quarterback off to the worst stretch of his career, and defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard is treating him like a problem anyway.

Buffalo's coaching staff met with reporters Monday to close the book on the Week 3 win over the Los Angeles Chargers and turn the page to the first divisional game of the season against the New England Patriots. The biggest topic was New England quarterback Drake Maye, who makes for a "tricky" evaluation this week, per Leonhard.

Maye was in the MVP conversation last season, ranking third in passing touchdowns (31), leading the NFL in passer rating (113.5), completion percentage (72%) and finished tied for lead in win percentage (.824). This against what many considered to be an easy schedule, before getting cooked by the Seattle Seahawks in the Super Bowl.

He has since thrown one touchdown pass against six interceptions and been sacked nine times through three games. That is a far cry from the player Leonhard spent late January getting ready to face in the AFC Championship.

"You turn on the tape from last year, and it was dynamic," the Bills DC said. "We played him in Denver, obviously at the end of the year, and you got to see the best version of what he was going into that game."

Last season, Maye threw for nearly 4,400 yards with 31 passing touchdowns and four rushing scores while carrying the Patriots to an AFC East title and a Super Bowl appearance. The playoffs went the other way: Denver held him without a touchdown and dropped him five times in the AFC Championship, and Seattle picked him off twice while sacking him six more times in the Super Bowl.

He sees the matchup against Buffalo as an opportunity to right the ship.

"This is an opportunity to band together and realize that the best football that we play is together and realizing that starts with me with protecting the football and protecting this team," Maye said. "That's my job, and I've been failing to do that."

Leonhard called Maye's postseason slide — four interceptions and 21 sacks across four games — "slip ups" next to "MVP level" regular-season film, and the struggles have bled into 2026. Maye and the Patriots arrive in Buffalo with the league's lowest-scoring offense at 12.0 points per game.

"You're watching a guy now that's you can tell he's going through some stuff and struggling a little bit, but at the same time he drops back and hits his top step and lets one rip and it's an explosive play," he added.

"You just have to put some pressure on him and hope that the trend continues. Great players are eventually going to come out the other side. You just hope it's after you play them."

The Bills head coach shared his thoughts on facing the Patriots QB with the press today as well.

"It is a week to week-to-week league, and it is so hard to play the position," Joe Brady said. "Drake Maye, he's an outstanding quarterback, he's played for so long at such a high level, he is going to present so many issues for us this week."

This article originally appeared on Bills Wire: Bills react to tough start for Patriots QB Drake Maye

title: Pennsylvania reports its 5th measles-related death of the year amid outbreak
description: A Parkside Pediatrics provider assessing a patient with measles symptoms in Spartanburg, South Carolina, on 30 January 2026.Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty...
fullText:
Pennsylvania has reported its fifth measles-associated death of 2026 as the state's ongoing outbreak climbs to 943 confirmed cases across 39 counties.

The Pennsylvania department of health said on Wednesday that an unvaccinated Lancaster county resident who tested positive for measles had died. Health officials did not release further information about the individual, citing privacy protections.

The death marks the fifth Pennsylvania resident to meet the state's definition of a measles-associated death this year after a fourth death two weeks ago. Due to how the Trump administration has changed its method for reporting measles deaths, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has not counted the Pennsylvania measles deaths in its national tally.

As of Monday 28 September, Pennsylvania had recorded 40 new positive cases. The outbreak has now reached 39 counties, with 943 cumulative confirmed cases, 176 hospitalizations and five confirmed measles-associated deaths.

Only four of those confirmed cases have involved vaccinated individuals, representing less than 1% of the state's total cases.

Health officials say daily totals can change, but monitoring the numbers gives residents and healthcare providers a clearer picture of community transmission across Pennsylvania and helps guide the state's response.

Agricultural communities in Lancaster and Mifflin counties have remained at the center of Pennsylvania's outbreak. Utah, Florida, Virginia and Texas have also reported dozens of cases, according to tracking from Johns Hopkins University.

Since the outbreak began in late April, staff at state health centers have administered more than 5,500 measles, mumps and rubella vaccine (MMR) vaccinations through 180 pop-up vaccination clinics in affected communities, according to a statement released on Wednesday.

Dozens of additional vaccination clinics are planned for the coming weeks and months, depending on community interest and need, the statement added.

More than 3,600 measles cases have been reported across the US in 2026, according to the CDC. The US eliminated measles in 2000, though it is unclear whether it can retain that status amid the recent outbreaks.

Measles is considered one of the most contagious diseases known to medicine. The MMR vaccine prevents 97% of measles cases.

Vaccination rates among kindergarten-aged children, which are considered an important indicator, have slowly declined as experts argue the Trump administration is promoting confusion and misinformation about vaccines among parents.

Earlier this month, Pennsylvania requested emergency assistance from the CDC in response to the measles outbreak, but warned that the request could be withdrawn unless the federal agency publicly recognized the measles-associated deaths reported by the state.

The dispute began after Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary and former head of an anti-vaccine advocacy group, publicly questioned whether the deaths linked to the measles outbreaks since he took office were caused by the virus or by another condition.

fullText:
The US Senate is set to leave Washington soon for election-season campaigning after two failed votes Wednesday on highly charged issues: AI data center costs and lawmakers' stock trading.

The Ratepayer Protection Act and the Stop Insider Trading Act were blocked by Democrats and fell short of the required 60 votes to advance in tallies of 57-43 and 53-47, respectively.

The data center bill garnered a handful of Democratic votes — but not enough to advance the legislation — while the stock trading bill failed on a party-line vote.

The political pattern around both bills was similar: Republicans charged Democrats with obstruction, while Democrats countered that both GOP-sponsored measures were bad-faith attempts to address serious issues.

Voters have strong feelings about the costs associated with data centers and insider trading by members of Congress. To that end, both sides staked out their campaign trail positions. Senate Majority Leader John Thune described the bills as "eminently commonsense pieces of legislation," while Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer shot back and called the data center bill "a fraud."

With a little over a month until the midterms, Democrats are bullish on their odds of winning majorities in Congress while Republicans search for ways to avoid a drubbing at the polls.

But on these issues at least, neither side will have results to show beyond the rhetoric.

On the Ratepayer Protection Act, Democrats aim to "prevent Republicans from gaining a political victory ahead of the midterms and hope that obstructionism does not resonate with voters," Stifel chief Washington policy strategist Brian Gardner wrote in a client note.

The votes on Wednesday afternoon are widely expected to be among the last before Senators go home to campaign. The House adjourned two weeks ago and is not scheduled to return to Washington until Nov. 9.

Republicans have been pushing a measure in recent months to limit, but not fully ban, lawmaker stock trading. President Trump even called for the measure's passage in his State of the Union address.

But the measure was dead on arrival among Democrats, as the bill was amended to include controversial election-related provisions that Trump has also called for.

The Stop Insider Trading Act would prohibit lawmakers and their families from purchasing new stocks, but it would allow lawmakers to continue owning individual stocks. It would also require a public notice at least seven days before any sale.

fullText:
Late-night hosts weighed in on Trump’s relationship with tech leaders and the White House’s new AI-powered site

On Tuesday night, late-night hosts discussed a Maha summit in Washington DC, the White House’s new AI-powered website and Donald Trump once again falling asleep on live TV.

On NBC, Seth Meyers focused on the president’s ill-phrased announcement of the US murder rate declining. “We have the best, uh, murder,” Trump said.

“What are you talking about, ‘We have the best murder’?” Meyers responded. “It’s a murder rate, not a murder rating.”

On Monday, Trump also took issue with the claim by the US ambassador to China, David Perdue, claim that he offered to sell weapons to China, saying: “I think he was probably talking about Taiwan.”

“So wait, are you saying that we have an ambassador to China who doesn’t know the difference between China and Taiwan?” asked Meyers. “That’s like if Mr Met showed up to the stadium wearing a Yankees jersey.”

Meanwhile, health officials in Florida have issued a local state of emergency after an outbreak of dengue fever. “Man, RFK Jr has only had the job two years and Florida is already turning into an episode of House,” the host laughed.

The White House has also rebuked criticism of taxpayer-funded TV ads. They said “they are public service announcements that are ‘reminding Americans to love their country’”, explained Meyers, before quipping: “The clearest sign of a healthy relationship is if you have to remind someone to love you.”

Trump reportedly told congressional leaders on Friday that he was revoking nearly $1bn in federal funding.

“Oh God, what’s he doing to the reflecting pool now?” joked Meyers. “Is he adding a waterslide?”

Meyers closed his monologue with news that the makers of a smart glasses brand have recalled frames after customers reported them overheating and causing burns.

“Well, I hate to break it to you,” he said, “but no matter what smart glasses you’re wearing, you’re gonna get burned.”

On Jimmy Kimmel Live! the host discussed Trump hosting all the top tech executives at the White House for a lunch on Tuesday. The guest list included Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman and the House speaker, Mike Johnson, “who was there to ask if there was any way that AI could turn him into a real boy”.

In a press conference, Trump announced that he was “changing the name” of AI from “artificial intelligence” to “superintelligence” “So far, everybody likes it,” he added.

“Yes,” responded Kimmel drily. “I’m sure the guy whose company’s name is OpenAI is very excited about this development.

“The idea that our guardrails against AI are being erected by an addled 80-year-old man … It’s like asking your grandpa to set up a wifi router in your house. You just wouldn’t do it.”

The host moved on to talk about the new AI-powered government website America.gov.

“A White House official called America.gov ‘a new front door for the federal government’,” said Kimmel. “You know, we need a new front door because Trump demolished the old front door to build his ballroom.”

Kimmel added that Trump is still trying to blame all of America’s struggles on his predecessor, again branding former president Joe Biden “sleepy” in Oval Office remarks this week. Ironically, Trump fell asleep shortly after.

“Only a few minutes after invoking the name ‘sleepy Joe Biden’, nappy Don Trump drifted off to dreamland on live TV,” Kimmel said.

This week also saw the second annual Maha summit in DC in an event attended by JD Vance, Robert F Kennedy Jr and Mike Tyson.

“You know we’re screwed when the sanest person in the group has half a face tattoo,” Kimmel said.

title: Oil shipments are recovering, but damaged refineries keep fuel prices high
description:
Crude oil is moving through the Strait of Hormuz at a pace that is starting to approach prewar levels, a notable rebound for the world’s most critical oil choke point. 
That restored flow is mainly the result of Iran’s somewhat depleted military capability and a U.S. Navy operation that has secured a portion of the waterway for relatively secure passage. 
Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post.
fullText:
Crude oil is moving through the Strait of Hormuz at a pace that is starting to approach prewar levels, a notable rebound for the world's most critical oil choke point.

That restored flow is mainly the result of Iran's somewhat depleted military capability and a U.S. Navy operation that has secured a portion of the waterway for relatively secure passage.

But the forces driving high fuel prices are not receding along with the development. That will require a lot more than the costly military campaign that is clearing the way for passage of one product at one particular moment in the war.

Most of the refined gasoline and diesel that was moving through the strait before the war is still not getting shipped, a major factor keeping prices elevated.

The rebound of crude shipments "is good news, but we are far from out of the woods," said Bob McNally, founder of the research firm Rapidan Energy Group. "The market realizes that. We have dug ourselves into a deep deficit over the last several months, and this only reduces it. It does not get us back to where we were."

Crude oil prices dipped Tuesday - largely as a response to Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline resuming limited operations. The price of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil, remained above $100 a barrel Wednesday morning, roughly 40 percent higher than it was when the Iran war began in February.

The outlook for the war and for oil was further clouded on Wednesday, when the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre reported that three vessels carrying fuel through a corridor of the strait the U.S. military has been trying to protect had been attacked the day before.

Meanwhile, the price of a gallon of regular gas in the United States is averaging $4.43, and diesel is at $6.41, according to AAA.

Analysts warn that even sustained deliveries of crude through the Strait of Hormuz at prewar levels would not do much to meaningfully bring down global prices in the coming weeks.

They note that oil inventories are depleted and need to be replenished. Refining infrastructure in the Middle East has been badly damaged and will take time to repair - all the while remaining vulnerable to further attacks.

As a result of that constrained capacity, gasoline and diesel shipments through the strait - crucial to bringing prices down for consumers - remain just a fraction of what they were before the war.

"Nobody consumes crude oil directly," said Mark Finley, an oil markets scholar at Rice University's Baker Institute for Public Policy. "It has to be made into something useful, like diesel or jet fuel or gasoline. The world's refining system that turns crude oil into useful products is severely strained."

As if to punctuate the point that the emergency is not over and inventories of everything are running low, the U.S. Energy Department on Tuesday announced it would release another 40 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which is already at its lowest level since 1983.

"We have dug ourselves into a big hole," Finley said.

There is general agreement in the oil industry that most of the crude still getting blocked in the Strait of Hormuz is Iranian, and that is by design. The U.S. is trying to put economic pressure on the regime and choke off its funding stream for its military activities.

As far as how much non-Iranian crude is getting through, ship tracking firms offer somewhat different estimates.

According to Kpler, the week ending Sept. 27 averaged nearly 12.5 million barrels per day, just 1 million barrels below the "pre-war baseline."

Windward, another ship tracking platform, estimated closer to 10 million barrels per day.

"This is not trivial," said Ami Daniel, Windward's co-founder and CEO. "The U.S. military has done a fantastic job facilitating consistent shipments."

The amount of oil getting through, though, does continue to swing wildly. There were days in September where only a few million barrels transited the strait, according to ship tracking data.

The restored flows depend on extremely costly U.S. Navy assistance and dark-fleet work-arounds that could unravel with a renewed Iranian military campaign.

Markets remain skeptical that the shipments of crude can continue at prewar levels absent a major diplomatic breakthrough between the U.S. and Iran.

"Maintaining the American military presence required to keep significant volumes of oil moving through the Strait comes at an enormous financial and operational cost," Danny Citrinowicz, a Middle East security scholar at the Atlantic Council, posted Tuesday on X.

"The real test is whether Washington can turn its military advantage into a durable situation in which oil flows normally, insurance and transportation costs decline, the extraordinary U.S. military deployment can be reduced, and Iran effectively loses Hormuz as a tool of strategic coercion," Citrinowicz wrote. "We are not there yet."

Even full restoration of shipping through the strait, McNally warned, would not bring markets back to where they were at the beginning of the year.

Iran has shifted its attacks away from the strait toward oil infrastructure on land, which in some cases can be even more damaging. One such recent attack disabled Saudi Arabia's key East-West pipeline, which had been delivering 7 million barrels of crude each day. The pipeline has been only partially restored, and analysts say it remains extremely vulnerable to further targeting.

"Iran may be losing control of Hormuz, but it retains the ability to disable critical infrastructure," McNally said. "This progress can be quickly offset by the Iranians and their allies hitting those fixed assets."

Karen DeYoung contributed to this report.

title: TSA officers can no longer sit while checking boarding passes and IDs
description:
Transportation Security Administration agents sit as they check boarding passes and IDs at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, on Monday, January 26, 2026. - Valerie Plesch/Bloomberg/Getty Images
Airport security employees checking boarding passes and IDs will no longer be allowed to sit down while working, the Transportation Security Administration confirmed Tuesday.
All chairs are being removed from the travel document checker podiums at the entrance to checkpoints nationwide, the union representing the screeners said. The American Federation of Government Employees TSA Council 100 said it found out about the decision from its members and called it a “disregard for workers rights and safety.”
TSA defended the move, saying the document checkers are the first to interact with the traveling public and requiring them to stand will create a better experience for passengers.
fullText:
Airport security employees checking boarding passes and IDs will no longer be allowed to sit down while working, the Transportation Security Administration confirmed Tuesday.

All chairs are being removed from the travel document checker podiums at the entrance to checkpoints nationwide, the union representing the screeners said. The American Federation of Government Employees TSA Council 100 said it found out about the decision from its members and called it a “disregard for workers rights and safety.”

TSA defended the move, saying the document checkers are the first to interact with the traveling public and requiring them to stand will create a better experience for passengers.

“This welcome change reinforces both our security posture and our commitment to hospitality by having these officers on their feet and alert,” the agency said in a statement. “All officers must meet fitness for duty requirements to be capable of performing their vital national security function while simultaneously creating a welcoming and professional environment for travelers.”

The move comes nearly two months after TSA Administrator David Cummins was confirmed to lead the agency.

The removal of chairs, the union said, has already begun in most commercial airports. There was no formal notification to AFGE or any of its local chapters, according to one union leader.

“These chairs serve as basic ergonomic and safety support for officers that stand and walk on hard surfaces all day,” the AFGE Council 100 statement read. “TSA is treating this matter like it is a privilege – it is not; it is basic safety and common decency for the workforce.”

As TSA approaches the 25th anniversary of its founding in November, Cummins has held meetings to “rapidly advance key strategic initiatives” as part of a program dubbed Horizon 25.

“TSA does not have to choose between a secure checkpoint, an efficient checkpoint, and an elevated passenger experience,” he said in a statement announcing the initiative.

The program includes expanding TSA PreCheck, rolling out new technology, privatizing some checkpoints and “improving the passenger experience.” It’s not clear whether requiring officers to stand while checking documents relates to this overhaul.

title: Trump had direct role in controversial taxpayer-funded ads, source says
description:
President Donald Trump speaks in the Oval Office of the White House, Monday, September 28, in Washington, DC. - Alex Brandon/AP

Coming just over a month before the November midterms, the ads have generated bipartisan criticism over how the Trump administration is spending taxpayer dollars.
“It’s a great message.
fullText:
President Donald Trump has personally driven the controversial, taxpayer-funded video ads promoting himself and his administration’s policies, including helping select the imagery and videos used, a source familiar with the matter told CNN.

Two Trump advisers familiar with the ads said that they were being created in-house by the White House video team — which is part of the communications team, responsible for the administration’s public messaging.

Coming just over a month before the November midterms, the ads have generated bipartisan criticism over how the Trump administration is spending taxpayer dollars.

“It’s a great message. I like the message, but it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters in the Capitol on Monday.

GOP Sen. John Cornyn of Texas echoed that sentiment: “It’s not even a close question.”

The White House has broadly defended the ads, saying they are akin to public service announcements past administrations have put out about Medicare, Obamacare and Covid-19 vaccinations. Officials have insisted they “are very clearly not campaign ads.”

“These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad,” a White House spokesperson said Monday.

But the imagery is undeniably meant to promote Trump, casting him as a warrior battling against existential threats. And the latest one appears nearly identical to a video Trump posted on Truth Social in January 2024, during his third presidential campaign.

That most recent ad shows Trump walking down a hall as audio plays of him saying “this is the final battle.”

“We will cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists. We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country. We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all,” Trump says in the ad, echoing comments he made during a Veterans Day speech in 2023.

The version on Truth Social has an additional six seconds that includes Trump’s campaign logo and a number to text. The text “Paid for by the US Government” is seen across the screen at the end of the new version of the ad.

Multiple members of Trump’s political operation said they were unaware that these ads were coming until they aired. But another source pushed back on the notion that anyone was kept in the dark — noting that the president had spoken about the ads to multiple aides and advisers and insisting that they were not being made in secret.

The latest ad — which aired during at least two NFL games on Sunday, during Fox’s broadcasts of the Washington Commanders-Seattle Seahawks matchup as well as the Carolina Panthers-Cleveland Browns game — is the third government-funded message in recent days to be captured by the media tracker AdImpact.

An ad that began airing Wednesday featured rapidly edited pictures and video of Trump over audio of him denouncing communism and socialism. Text on the screen touted his administration’s accomplishments, including “reigniting American manufacturing.”

“The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic,” a White House spokesperson said in a statement. “We should be proud of our country.”

The music used in that ad — a song called “Love Me” by JMSN — has also come under scrutiny. Lawyers for the artist sent White House chief of staff Susie Wiles a letter on Monday asking the administration to “immediately withdraw the advertisement from all scheduled airings” and “cease and desist any use of the Song and/or any of the intellectual property of JMSN.”

A second ad features video of Trump at Mount Rushmore as his voice is heard saying, “Never before has any nation celebrated so magnificent a triumph as this one.”

Beyond questions of intellectual property, watchdog groups say the ads mark a clear violation of appropriations law restricting the use of federal funding for propaganda or partisan communications.

“The most immediate check on this kind of behavior is supposed to be and needs to be Congress. Congress has not asserted itself as the first branch of government with the power of the purse to hold the president accountable,” said Donald Sherman, president and CEO of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics, or CREW, in Washington.

GOP lawmakers may be hesitant to provide accountability, he added, because the ads “are designed to boost Republicans in Congress,” he said.

And, Sherman noted, the Government Accountability Office — the nonpartisan agency that would be tasked with investigations into this type of issue — is currently without Senate-confirmed leadership.

“That makes it that much harder for them to move with speed to address a high-profile and politically sensitive investigation like this requires,” he said.

Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, said in a post on X that the ads “may be felony criminal theft and conversion of government property for political campaign purposes.”

And Raskin, who will gain congressional subpoena power in November if Democrats win the House, said it is not just Trump who might face inquiries over the messages. He said the creation of the ads was a “Hatch Act violation for any government employees who worked on it or used government resources to make it.”

“This is dumb, dumb, dumb beyond belief,” one former Trump campaign official told CNN. “These guys are all gonna get subpoenaed. It’s gonna be bad.”

The story has been updated with additional information.

CNN’s Kit Maher contributed to this report.

fullText:
President Trump gathered top artificial intelligence leaders in Washington on Tuesday and doubled down on his opposition to government intervention, suggesting that "self-regulation" is the answer to growing worries about the technology getting out of human control.

"There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation," the president said after meeting with the assembled CEOs. "There was a lot of commonality in this room."

Trump said he and the CEOs signed a "morally binding" accord that wasn't immediately released but that the president said would keep the companies in line through "self-policing and group policing."

Some executives on hand said the so-called Accord on Super Intelligence would include commitments to a combination of technological controls to detect problems with new models, internal risk review efforts, external auditors, and other measures.

Meta (META) CEO Mark Zuckerberg called the accord "a start," while others suggested some details still needed to be worked out.

"The mechanism, how we address those risks, is still under discussion," Anthropic (ANTH.PVT) CEO Dario Amodei said. Progress had been made toward both the US winning AI and also winning safely, he said, though he emphasized that the technology still poses "real dangers."

Amodei published an essay earlier this month titled "We Must Pace the Frontier," which set off a fierce debate about the need for a cooperative slowdown in AI capability.

The accord also formally changed the name of the technology in government record-keeping to Super Intelligence.

"We've changed the name officially to SI," Trump said.

The "meeting and luncheon on Super Intelligence," as the White House described the event, took place in the East Room, with Trump even posting the seating chart. The location was the same spot where just a few days ago, many of the same AI leaders gathered for a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Elon Musk of Tesla (TSLA), Jensen Huang of Nvidia (NVDA), and Lisa Su of Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) were all at the head table with Xi last Thursday and again received prominent spots near Trump.

After the meeting, Trump also said he was "very close" to a decision on an AI czar and would announce it in the next three to four days.

Other notable guests included Google (GOOGL, GOOG) CEO Sundar Pichai, Microsoft (MSFT) CEO Satya Nadella, OpenAI (OPAI.PVT) president Greg Brockman, Palantir (PLTR) CEO Alex Karp, Amazon (AMZN) founder Jeff Bezos, and others.

The gathering came as the US continues to digest a raft of alarming new AI disclosures in recent days, such as an Axios report that OpenAI, Anthropic, and security researchers were sifting through thousands of incidents of problematic actions by AI agents.

title: President Trump launches new AI-powered government website
description:
President Donald Trump launched America.gov on Tuesday, unveiling what the administration has billed as a new AI-powered gateway to federal information and services that aims to streamline Americans’ interactions with the government.
The website, which Trump introduced at Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium in Washington, features a chatbot-style interface that allows users to ask questions about government programs, benefits and services. The administration described America.
fullText:
President Donald Trump launched America.gov on Tuesday, unveiling what the administration has billed as a new AI-powered gateway to federal information and services that aims to streamline Americans' interactions with the government.

The website, which Trump introduced at Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium in Washington, features a chatbot-style interface that allows users to ask questions about government programs, benefits and services. The administration described America.gov as a "front door" to federal resources, consolidating information that is currently spread across dozens of agency websites.

"It's not just simply a website. It's a restoration of America's founding promise, and it's a reinvention of your government for the 21st century and beyond," Trump said at the rollout.

The debut of America.gov comes as policymakers, technology companies and privacy advocates continue to debate the expanding role of artificial intelligence in public-facing services. While AI tools have been touted for their ability to simplify complex tasks and improve access to information, experts have raised concerns about accuracy, transparency and data privacy, particularly when such systems are used to help people access government programs or services.

Asked at the announcement about risks associated with AI and centralized government services, Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz told Newsweek the administration does not want all user data stored in a single location. Instead, he described America.gov as a "federated system" in which individuals maintain control of their own records and choose whether to share them. Oz acknowledged that any system allowing access to sensitive information carries risks, but said federal officials are prioritizing cybersecurity and data protection as the platform evolves.

"We don't want all the information in one link," Oz said. "The real risk we have is if all your data is in one spot ... anyone who hacks it gets it all."

The president said Tuesday, "It cannot in theory be hacked into. And when they figure a way to do that, we'll end it, because they always figure a way, right?"

Joe Gebbia, U.S. chief design officer, said America.gov is powered by Google's Gemini and Elon Musk's Grok. Trump was joined by Musk, administration officials and tech leaders for the announcement.

Newsweek has reached out to the White House via email on Tuesday morning for comment.

Trump signed an executive order Tuesday that directs federal agencies to integrate their online services with America.gov, which the administration envisions as a single digital portal for accessing government information and completing transactions.

The White House said the platform will eventually allow users to perform tasks such as renewing passports and enrolling in Medicare, while Login.gov, the federal government's existing sign-in system, will be incorporated into the service.

The order applies to public-facing federal services used by more than 100,000 people annually, although IRS tax-filing services and certain national security-related functions are excluded.

"This is the American government working for the American people. Come to America.gov, tell us what you need. We'll help you get there and, ultimately, we'll help you get it done," Edward Frost, Administrator of the U.S. General Services Administration (GSA), told Newsweek at Tuesday's announcement.

The launch of America.gov also highlights the growing influence of Gebbia, the Airbnb co-founder whom Trump tapped in 2025 to lead the newly created National Design Studio. Established under the administration's "America by Design" initiative, the office is responsible for modernizing federal websites and digital services.

The chatbot-based America.gov portal represents one of the most visible examples of Gebbia's effort to apply Silicon Valley-style design principles to the federal government.

The launch of America.gov coincides with a high-profile White House gathering of some of the technology industry's most influential executives.

Trump will host a lunch focused on AI shortly after unveiling the new portal Attendees include Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora and Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner.

The technology leaders joined Vice President JD Vance, House Speaker Mike Johnson, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. The meeting comes as artificial intelligence is playing an increasingly prominent role in both the private and public sectors, with governments around the world grappling with how to harness the technology while addressing concerns about accuracy, privacy and security.

Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.

Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gabe Whisnant and Dave Siminoff.

title: Reports surface that Netanyahu ignored Oct. 7 attack warnings to dominate Israeli election
description:
JERUSALEM - A slew of reports that Arab officials warned Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu about a serious threat emerging from Gaza days before the Oct. 7, 2023, attack by Hamas have put the longtime Israeli leader on the defensive less than 30 days before a pivotal election. 
Ever since the attack, the most deadly in Israel’s history, Netanyahu has argued that Israeli security chiefs collectively failed to foresee the surprise attack by Hamas - but that he led the fightback, scoring redemptive battlefield victories in Gaza, Lebanon, Syria and Iran.
Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. 
But that narrative is fraying as reports of the advance warnings, including one delivered by United Arab Emirates President Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan, train a spotlight on Netanyahu’s handling of the attack and his refusal to allow an independent commission to investigate it.
fullText:
JERUSALEM - A slew of reports that Arab officials warned Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu about a serious threat emerging from Gaza days before the Oct. 7, 2023, attack by Hamas have put the longtime Israeli leader on the defensive less than 30 days before a pivotal election.

Ever since the attack, the most deadly in Israel's history, Netanyahu has argued that Israeli security chiefs collectively failed to foresee the surprise attack by Hamas - but that he led the fightback, scoring redemptive battlefield victories in Gaza, Lebanon, Syria and Iran.

But that narrative is fraying as reports of the advance warnings, including one delivered by United Arab Emirates President Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan, train a spotlight on Netanyahu's handling of the attack and his refusal to allow an independent commission to investigate it.

Netanyahu and his office have denied the reports, and his political party and supporters have accused "left-wing" Israeli officials, as well as journalists and overseas interests, of conspiring to oust him from office through a coordinated smear campaign ahead of the Oct. 27 election.

The disclosures began to trickle out in early September, when the Israeli newspaper Haaretz published an excerpt from "Hostages: 843 Days of Abandonment," a book by two Israeli journalists that details an encrypted call reportedly made by the Emirati president, who is known as MBZ, less than two weeks before Oct. 7, 2023, to warn Netanyahu that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was planning a major operation that could destabilize the Middle East. Netanyahu did not pass on the warnings to his security aides, according to the book authors, Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval.

"We have excellent proof and many more scoops in the book," Eldar said. "It's rock solid." The UAE Foreign Ministry did not deny the Haaretz excerpt, saying, "When necessary, all relevant intelligence has been and continues to be communicated between the relevant entities."

In recent days, the debate in Israel has reached a fever pitch after the Atlantic and the Wall Street Journal published reports that then-Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel also warned Netanyahu about Gaza in the days before Oct. 7.

On Sunday, Netanyahu flew to Abu Dhabi and requested that MBZ explicitly deny that a warning call about Oct. 7 took place in late 2023, said a person with knowledge of the meeting who, like others quoted in this article, spoke on the condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter.

Netanyahu's office denied that Netanyahu made such a request, calling it "fake news." When asked about the Sunday meeting, the UAE Foreign Ministry referred The Washington Post to a report by the official Emirates News Agency released late Monday saying the two leaders had discussed "bilateral relations and ways to strengthen ties." The ministry declined further comment.

Several senior Israeli officials, including the former army chief of staff and head of military intelligence, have resigned, saying they failed to protect the country.

Netanyahu, by contrast, has deflected responsibility and repeatedly accused his security chiefs of missing the threat from Gaza and even "deliberately" letting him sleep for four hours after Hamas began its assault on southern Israel at 6:30 a.m. on Oct. 7.

On Monday, Ronen Bar, the former director of Shin Bet, Israel's domestic intelligence agency, sued Netanyahu for defamation, accusing the prime minister of "trying to deflect fire from himself by hurling accusations at the person who warned him in real time."

It's not immediately clear how the allegations will affect polls, which have held relatively steady in recent weeks and show former military chief Gadi Eisenkot's party narrowly leading Netanyahu's Likud. The reports, however, have dominated headlines and prime-time talk shows.

Several security branches, including the Israel Defense Forces and Shin Bet, have conducted internal probes into their failures to anticipate the Oct. 7 attack, but Netanyahu's government has refused to authorize one for itself.

Many of Netanyahu's campaign rivals, including Eisenkot, have pledged to immediately establish an independent commission of inquiry if elected.

Jonathan Rynhold, a political scientist at Bar-Ilan University, said Netanyahu may be hobbled by the claims about the warnings, but his loyal base and Israel's predominantly right-leaning voters may not jump ship for the centrist bloc led by Eisenkot without a "clear smoking gun."

"Oct. 7 has been on everybody's mind every day for three years, so it is relevant, but these claims have been bubbling for a long time in different forms," Rynhold said. "Imagine there's a video of all the Egyptians and the Emiratis and you can actually see him getting the warning and it was repeated 50 times on social media, then it becomes unavoidable. But obviously that's not what's going to happen."

Sufian Abu Zaida, a former Palestinian official who was the source of the warning that eventually reached the UAE, told The Post that he met Sinwar, the Hamas leader, in his Gaza City office in September 2023, and Sinwar dictated an offer to Israeli negotiators: he would release two Israeli soldiers and two civilians held in Gaza in exchange for Israel freeing Palestinian prisoners and lifting its heavy trade and movement restrictions imposed on the strip since 2007. Otherwise, Sinwar warned, there would be an "earthquake."

"The exact content of the message was: "We will put cards on the table, there will be an earthquake regarding the negotiations and we will empty the [Israeli] prisons [of Palestinians]," Abu Zaida recalled in an interview this week, adding that Sinwar told him to "make sure" the message reached the Israelis.

Abu Zaida said he passed the message to Shin Bet officials and also relayed it to an adviser to MBZ in Abu Dhabi - the Palestinian politician Mohammad Dahlan, who then informed the UAE president. Abu Zaida said he also passed the message to Samir al-Mashharawi, a Palestinian political leader and Dahlan associate based in Egypt.

The three Palestinian intermediaries "didn't know that Sinwar was ready to go ahead with his threats, or how and when," Abu Zaida said. "I was thinking that it might be about the West Bank: kidnapping a soldier from here or there for later negotiations with Israel for a prisoner exchange."

Several months after Oct. 7, in early 2024, MBZ recounted to then-CIA Director William J. Burns that he had warned Netanyahu about the possibility of violence erupting but did not include specific details that anticipated the Oct. 7 plot, a person familiar with the matter said.

The Emirates' refusal to disavow the reports of advance warnings is particularly striking because it is the Arab country that has stood closest to Netanyahu over the past three years even as his international standing plummeted.

Since signing the Abraham Accords that normalized diplomatic relations with Israel in 2020, the UAE has often been more measured in its criticism of Israel's conduct in Gaza and the West Bank than some other Arab countries that have accused Israel of genocide and ethnic cleansing.

At other times, the UAE has taken a relatively tougher stance toward Israel's foes, such as Iran, and it has supported the U.S.-Israeli-led war.

Alex Vatanka, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute in Washington, noted that Emirati officials have declined to hand Netanyahu a political favor by explicitly denying the reports of the warnings.

"The reality is that Netanyahu is a liability for the UAE right now," Vatanka said. "They are sensitive to their image in the Islamic world and don't want to be seen as too close with Netanyahu."

But, he added, the UAE is "not going to walk away from its relationship" with the state of Israel itself.

Back home, Netanyahu's supporters kicked into damage-control mode.

"As the elections approach, we are seeing a flood of false reports by mobilized left-wing journalists, aimed at toppling the right and installing a Left-Muslim Brotherhood government that will surrender on every front," the Likud Party said in a statement.

Amit Segal, a political commentator who is seen as close to Netanyahu, said there were "Arab nations" behind the "slanderous fabrications" and warned that if the Israeli right lost the elections, a Palestinian state would emerge.

"This is the election question: It is either the Right or Palestine," Segal posted on social media.

Eldar, the Israeli author, said Likud lawyers have threatened to sue him for defamation and accused him of seeking to influence the election. He said he first obtained information about the call almost two years ago and it took the publisher until this month to release the book.

"I would have preferred to publish it a year ago, but it took time," Eldar said.

One Israeli political consultant, who is not affiliated with a campaign in this election cycle and who spoke on the condition of anonymity to preserve client relationships, said Netanyahu's campaign might find ways to benefit from the fallout of the new claims.

The controversy could draw attention away from the intense criticism Netanyahu has faced over his government's policy of allowing ultra-Orthodox Jews to forgo mandatory military service, and Netanyahu could instead focus attention on Oct. 7 and the danger posed by Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about 21 percent of the Israeli population, the consultant said.

Polls show that to form a majority government, Eisenkot may need to join hands with the so-called Arab parties, which Netanyahu's campaign has frequently portrayed as security risks in campaign ads with racist undertones.

The furor over the pre-Oct. 7 warnings "seems negative, but it's also changed the narrative" in Israel, the consultant said. "Netanyahu can push aside the ultra-Orthodox issue and bring to the table the conversation about the fact that Gadi Eisenkot doesn't have a majority without the voice or fingers of the Arab parties."

Lior Soroka contributed to this report.

fullText:
Washington — President Trump on Monday announced that the company Mesabi Metallics will build a $15 billion steel plant in Iowa over the coming years, in what would be the largest of its kind in U.S. history.

"There's a company known as Mesabi," the president said in the Oval Office. "And they're going to make a big investment in a place called Iowa. I love Iowa. I won Iowa every time. Today, we're thrilled to announce that Mesabi Metallics will be building the largest steel plant in American history in the great state of Iowa."

The president and the Minnesota-based Mesabi Metallics unveiled the company's plans for what the White House is calling a mega steel plant, alongside Mesabi executives and Iowa officials. The announcement comes as several Iowa Republicans face competitive elections in the November midterms, including the party's candidates for Senate and governor.

Although Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said Monday the steel plant won't receive direct federal support, he acknowledged that the government-run Export-Import Bank financed Mesabi's iron ore plant in Minnesota, which will provide the raw materials essential to making steel.

Once it's up and running in 2030, the plant is expected to produce 7.5 million or more tons of steel per year. A White House official said the plant is expected to create 1,750 permanent jobs in Iowa.

The plans for a new plant mark the Trump administration's latest move to boost domestic steel manufacturing in the face of overseas competition, a centerpiece of the president's trade agenda. Last year, he doubled tariffs on imported steel to 50%, and steel levies have been part of the ongoing trade dispute between the U.S. and Canada. He also approved a deal for Japan-based Nippon Steel to buy U.S. Steel, an arrangement that calls for new investments in the iconic Pittsburgh-based company.

Mesabi has not announced where in Iowa the steel plant will be, but Energy Secretary Chris Wright mentioned that it would be in the southeast part of the state. A White House official said this will be the first mega steel plant built in the U.S. since the 1960s. The Trump administration expects the steel could support U.S. defense projects in the future. The Wall Street Journal was first to report the president's anticipated announcement of the new steel plant.

The Export-Import Bank's board approved a $770 million direct loan to Mesabi Metallics for its iron ore endeavors on Sept. 24, a spokesperson for EXIM told CBS News. The board was initially considering up to $10 billion in support, according to a March news release.

Mesabi Metallics is owned by India-based Essar Group, but its operations haven't always been known as Mesabi Metallics.

In 2008, the Essar Group's Essar Steel Minnesota LLC began work on a massive iron mine and processing facility in Minnesota. But after years of delays, missed deadlines and financial challenges, Essar Steel Minnesota LLC filed for bankruptcy in 2016. Frustrated with the delays, the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources took steps in 2019 to potentially bar Essar Global from working with the state, although the company sued over that move, and the state ultimately did not complete the debarment process.

"This is a step in the right direction after northern Minnesotans have waited patiently — too patiently, in fact — for economic gains that have been dangled in front of their eyes for many years," Democratic state Reps. Julie Sandstede and Rob Ecklund said in a statement at the time.

What was known as Essar Steel Minnesota LLC was eventually reborn from the ashes of bankruptcy and was bought by Chippewa Capital Partners. But Essar Group eventually regained control starting in 2019.

CBS News has reached out to Mesabi Metallics and the Essar Group for comment.

State aid could potentially be on the way for Mesabi Metallics, too.

The Des Moines Register reported state lawmakers are being alerted they may need to return to the statehouse to approve tax breaks for Mesabi. CBS News has reached out to top members of the Iowa statehouse for comment.

"I'm so excited about this project," Iowa Sen. Joni Ernst said, thanking Mr. Trump and Essar.

It's not clear why the steel plant is in Iowa, instead of Minnesota, closer to the iron ore mine.

Iowa Republicans are facing competitive races for the U.S. House, Senate and governor's mansion. Republicans, who currently hold the governor's mansion and both Senate seats, are trying to fend off Democrats from changing that.

In the governor's race, Democratic Iowa State Auditor Rob Sand is facing off against Republican businessman Zach Lahn in what's expected to be a close race. In the open U.S. Senate seat being vacated by Sen. Joni Ernst's departure, Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson faces Democratic state lawmaker Josh Turek.

In the House, there are closely watched races in two Iowa congressional districts, between Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Democratic former state Rep. Christina Bohannan, and between Republican Rep. Zach Nunn and Democratic state Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott.

Mr. Trump gave Hinson a shoutout in the Oval Office Monday, saying she will be "hopefully elected to the Senate, and she's outstanding." The president said he'll visit Iowa for a "great rally" there before the midterms.

A reporter asked the president why Republicans are having to work so hard to win seats in Iowa, a state he won by 13 points. The president said he thinks the polls, which show close statewide races in the Hawkeye State, are inaccurate.

"I don't know, I love Iowa," he said. "I've always been very strong with Iowa."

description:

Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. 
Bailey, who was hired for the leadership role about a year ago, confirmed his departure in a social media post.
fullText:
The conservative firebrand whom the Trump administration installed as a No. 2 at the FBI announced Monday that he is resigning from the bureau.

Andrew Bailey, the former Missouri attorney general who has supported debunked claims that the 2020 election was stolen, told bureau employees in an email that he was leaving to spend more time with this family, according to three people familiar with the personnel move who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a matter they were not authorized to speak about.

Bailey, who was hired for the leadership role about a year ago, confirmed his departure in a social media post.

"With great pride in what we have accomplished, I am announcing that I am stepping down to return to my family in Missouri," Bailey wrote on social media. "I am confident Director Patel will continue to reform the FBI, combat violent crime, defend the homeland, ensure strong organizational accountability, and restore public trust in this institution of excellence."

The departure marks a dramatic turn for Bailey, a loyalist of President Donald Trump who had been floated as a candidate early in the administration to run the FBI or Justice Department.

It is also the latest shake-up at the federal law enforcement agency under FBI Director Kash Patel. Bailey was hired to serve as the co-deputy director alongside Dan Bongino, a conservative podcast host and former Secret Service officer.

Neither Bongino nor Bailey had FBI experience, which made them highly unusual picks for a position that typically goes to a veteran of the bureau. The position does not require Senate confirmation and is tasked with running the day-to-day operations of the FBI.

Earlier this year, Bongino quit amid frustrations about the demands of the position, The Washington Post previously reported. He was replaced with Christopher Raia, a career FBI official.

During Bailey's tenure, the department has seen an unprecedented wave of dismissals and transfers of experienced FBI agents.

Last week, for example, the top two agents running the counterterrorism division in the Washington field office were transferred because of their work investigating threats against Katie Miller - a conservative podcaster who is the wife of top Trump aide Stephen Miller - according to three people familiar with the matter.

The officials were transferred because top officials felt work on the probe was moving too slowly, said the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a personnel matter.

Bailey resigned from his position as Missouri attorney general last September to assume the role as FBI co-deputy director.

He is a military veteran who as Missouri's chief legal officer mounted high-profile legal fights aligned with Trump's agenda. He sued Starbucks over its diversity, equity and inclusion policies; fought transgender care policies; and waged legal battles against "sanctuary city" policies.

Among the most notable parts of Bailey's short FBI tenure was his presence on the scene as the FBI executed search warrants in January to seize 2020 ballots and other election material from Fulton County, Georgia.

It is rare for an FBI deputy director to personally oversee such a routine development in an investigation, but Bailey's presence was also notable given the political tensions surrounding the probe and Trump's repeated insistence, without evidence, that the 2020 election was stolen. The FBI has said it is investigating whether what it has described in court filings as "deficiencies" in the 2020 vote tabulation in Fulton County, home to Atlanta, were the result of intentional wrongdoing that could constitute a crime.

title: Trump asked China's Xi if he wants to buy U.S. arms, ambassador says
description: — President Donald Trump has justified the pending U.S. arms sale to Taiwan to Chinese President Xi Jinping by downplaying it as just one of many sales Washington makes around the world — even asking Xi if he’d be in the market for U.S. arms, Trump’s ambassador to China said on Sunday.
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump has justified the pending U.S. arms sale to Taiwan to Chinese President Xi Jinping by downplaying it as just one of many sales Washington makes around the world — even asking Xi if he'd be in the market for U.S. arms, Trump's ambassador to China said on Sunday.

David Perdue said Trump raised the prospect of the arms sales from the U.S. to its ascendant geopolitical rival, an unlikely offer that if consummated would upend generations of U.S. policy toward China and Taiwan and potentially expose U.S. technology to a potential foe. Perdue, speaking to Shannon Bream on "Fox News Sunday" days after Trump hosted Xi for a state visit in Washington, didn't specify when the offer was made.

Bream had cited concerns from Republican and Democratic lawmakers over delayed aid packages and weapons orders to Taiwan, the self-ruled democracy, to defend itself from China's threat to invade the island. Bream asked if the U.S. is denying arms to Taiwan to appease the Chinese president, who visited Trump last week.

Perdue pushed back on the suggestion, stating that Trump "is as strong on Taiwan as I've ever seen anybody" and has sold it plenty of weapons. Perdue also said Trump and Xi continue to talk about future U.S. weapons sales to Taiwan.

"But President Trump continues to say, 'Hey, we sell arms to other people around the world,'" Perdue said. "He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some, at one point."

The U.S. is bound by its own laws to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself. While not recognizing Taiwan as a country, the U.S. is the island's strongest informal backer and arms provider. But multiple U.S. leaders have left ambiguous whether they would commit military force to defend the U.S. ally should China invade.

China has pressed Washington to halt the arms sales, most prominently during a previous summit in May between Trump and Xi in Beijing. After that meeting, the United States paused the sale of a record-breaking $14 billion package — and Trump described arms sales to Taiwan as a "very good negotiating chip" with China.

In their private talks at the White House last week, Xi pressed Trump to oppose Taiwan independence, according to Chinese state media.

In Beijing, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun did not confirm Perdue's remarks when asked about the matter on Monday. But he told reporters that China has always strengthened its national defense capabilities based on its needs, and is committed to maintaining world peace and stability.
